The spotted ground squirrel (Xerospermophilus spilosoma) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that are characteristic of small, arid-adapted sciurids. Under the thermal conditions typical of its active season (35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]), females give birth to a single litter per year, with litter sizes ranging from 4 to 12 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4 to 12 pups per litter] and a single litter produced annually [F_R_i = single litter produced annually]. This modest reproductive output likely reflects the constraints of a hot, unpredictable environment where energetic demands are high. The maximum observed reproductive rate for this species is therefore one litter per year. Neonates are altricial, with a birth mass estimated at 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams] based on data from the congener Xerospermophilus mohavensis.

The timing of early developmental events in X. spilosoma is tightly linked to the warm conditions of the late spring and summer. Under the species' typical thermal conditions (35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]), gestation proceeds for 24 days [tg = 24 days] and the pre-weaning interval lasts 21 days since birth [tx = 21 days since birth]. This rapid weaning age allows the young to begin foraging independently before the onset of the hottest part of the summer, when surface activity becomes energetically costly for small mammals.

Adult female spotted ground squirrels attain a typical ultimate body mass of 150 grams [Wwi = 150 grams], though individuals may range between 100 and 200 grams depending on local resource availability and seasonal fattening. This body size is moderate among the diminutive ground squirrels of the genus Xerospermophilus and is associated with a relatively low resting metabolic rate. Maximal basal oxygen consumption in this species has been recorded at 88.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 88.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured under controlled laboratory conditions at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Such a low metabolic rate is an adaptation to the hot, xeric habitats this species occupies, reducing both water loss and the need for extensive foraging.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Xerospermophilus spilosoma is delayed relative to the pace of its early growth. Females typically reach puberty at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth], meaning they do not breed until their second calendar year following birth at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This delay aligns with the species' single annual reproductive event and the energetic requirements of surviving a long, hot summer and a period of winter torpor. The lifespan of the spotted ground squirrel, approximated from data on the Mohave ground squirrel at the same thermal reference of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], is about 7.8 years [am = about 7.8 years]. This longevity is moderately high for a rodent of its size and likely reflects a slow pace of life with low adult mortality in a relatively stable, if harsh, environment.

Ecologically, the spotted ground squirrel is an obligate burrow-dweller of sandy soils in the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts. Its activity above ground is largely confined to the morning and late afternoon hours during the warmer months, as the species avoids the lethal heat of midday. The squirrels are dietary generalists, consuming seeds, green vegetation, and insects as they become seasonally available. Unlike some ground squirrels that undergo prolonged hibernation, this species may experience a period of summer estivation in the hottest months, a behavior that reduces the seasonal window for reproduction to a single annual event.
